proposal.comment: [Playbook] The agreement has no indemnification section at all, although Sections 9.3, 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5 assume one (including a dangling reference to Section 20.5). We have inserted our standard Vendor indemnity (IP infringement, breach of law, Vendor-caused data breach, gross negligence/wilful misconduct) with the usual notice/control procedure and procure-modify-replace-refund remedies, and kept our own indemnity narrow.

ops.text: Vendor shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Customer shall give prompt notice of the claim, and Vendor shall control the defence and may not settle in a manner imposing obligations on Customer without its consent. If the Services or a Deliverable are alleged to infringe, Vendor shall, at its expense, procure the right to continue use, modify or replace the affected item so that it is non-infringing and materially equivalent, or, failing that, refund the Fees paid for the affected item (Section 20.5 remedies). Customer's only indemnity obligation is for third-party claims arising from Customer-provided content or Customer's breach of Applicable Law.

proposal.summary: Insert Vendor indemnity (Section 20) after the warranty section.

quote: Customer may terminate an Order Form immediately if Vendor suffers a material Security Incident, repeatedly misses a critical service level, violates Applicable Law in performing the Services, or infringes a third party's intellectual property and cannot provide the remedies required by Section 20.5.
rationale: There is no indemnification section anywhere in the agreement (numbering jumps from 19 to 21), yet Sections 9.3, 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5 all assume one, including a dangling cross-reference to "Section 20.5". With no Vendor IP indemnity at all this is walk-away territory, so we have inserted our standard Vendor indemnity with notice/control procedure, infringement remedies and a narrow Customer indemnity.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We own what we pay for: Deliverables are created specifically for us, so Vendor ownership with only a revocable, term-limited licence is not acceptable (and sits oddly with the perpetual licence in Section 13.2). We have reversed the assignment and added a licence-back fallback; Vendor Technology remains Vendor's under Section 14.3.

ops.newText: Customer exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer, and Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all right, title and interest in each Deliverable upon creation. To the extent any such assignment is ineffective, Vendor grants Customer and its Affiliates a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid, transferable licence to use, modify and sublicense the Deliverable for Customer's business.
ops.oldText: Vendor exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer. Customer receives a revocable, non-transferable licence to use a Deliverable only during the applicable Order Form term.

proposal.summary: Give Customer ownership of Deliverables with a perpetual licence fallback.

quote: Vendor exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer. Customer receives a revocable, non-transferable licence to use a Deliverable only during the applicable Order Form term.
rationale: Section 14.1 correctly leaves Customer Data and our pre-existing IP with us, but Section 14.2 gives Vendor exclusive ownership of Deliverables built specifically for us with only a revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence back — below the fallback (which requires at least a perpetual, irrevocable, sublicensable licence) and in tension with Section 13.2. We reversed the assignment and added a perpetual licence fallback; Vendor Technology stays with Vendor under Section 14.3.

quote: Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 meets our preferred position: a mutual cap at the greater of 12 months' Fees paid or payable and USD 1,000,000, a mutual consequential-damages exclusion (with data restoration and replacement services preserved as direct damages), Excluded Claims covering confidentiality, data protection, security, indemnities, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement, and confirmation that our payment obligation is not "damages". Section 18.2 confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liability, so the cap is not undercut in our disfavour.

rationale: Preferred position met: Section 24.1 lets us assign to Affiliates and successors without consent, Section 24.2 restricts Vendor assignment (consent not unreasonably withheld, never to a Customer competitor), and Section 24.4 removes any Vendor right arising on our change of control. Section 13.3 confirms licence transferability.

rationale: No exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation binds us; Section 12.3 expressly preserves our freedom to engage any supplier. The only quasi-exclusivity feature is the match/right-of-first-refusal in Section 7.2, which we have redlined under MFN rather than flagging the same term twice.

The nearest penalty-like exposure is the Section 2.1 take-or-pay, which we have addressed under MINCOMMIT rather than double-flagging here.

The narrower Deliverable licence in Section 14.2 is addressed under the IP rule rather than flagged twice here.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept restrictions on the products or businesses we may build, buy or sell, and a 24-month, all-territory competition ban also contradicts Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that no non-compete has been given. We have deleted it; if some protection is genuinely needed we could look at a narrow, term-only restriction tied to a named competing product with carve-outs for internal development and acquisitions.

quote: During the term and for twenty-four months thereafter, Customer shall not develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory.
rationale: Section 12.4 (second instance) imposes an undefined-scope, all-territory, 24-month post-term non-compete on us — beyond the fallback and squarely in walk-away territory — and it contradicts Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges no non-compete has been given. Deleted.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 9 gives only for-cause, insolvency and performance-based termination rights, and Section 2.1 expressly denies any termination right across a three-year term. We need a convenience right on 30 days' notice with a pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees; our fallback is 60-90 days' notice with any early-termination fee capped at three months' Fees.

ops.text: Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience, in whole or in part, upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor, in which case Vendor shall refund any prepaid Fees for the period after the effective date of termination and no early-termination charge applies. Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or an Order Form for convenience during a committed term.

proposal.summary: Add a Customer termination-for-convenience right on 30 days' notice with refund of prepaid Fees.

quote: Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.
rationale: The three-year term in Section 8.1 comes with only for-cause, insolvency, security/service-level and force-majeure termination rights (Sections 9.1–9.5, 27.3); no Customer termination for convenience exists anywhere, and Section 2.1 expressly denies termination rights. Absence of a convenience right in a multi-year term is a walk-away, so we inserted a 30-day right with a pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 7.2 requires us to disclose and match third-party offers before engaging another provider — an open-ended MFN plus right of first refusal running against us, and inconsistent with Section 12.3's acknowledgement that no most-favoured-customer commitment has been made. We have deleted it; MFN pricing in our favour remains welcome.

quote: Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
rationale: Section 7.2 is an open-ended MFN running against us: we must disclose any more favourable third-party offer and give Vendor a match right before engaging another provider. That is walk-away territory (unlimited scope, no time limit, no comparison carve-outs) and it conflicts with Section 12.3's no-most-favoured-customer acknowledgement. Deleted; Vendor-granted MFN remains welcome.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] A three-year, USD 2,000,000 per year take-or-pay with no reduction or termination right is a walk-away for us, and it contradicts Section 12.3's acknowledgement that no minimum-volume commitment has been made. We have limited any commitment to the current 12-month term, made it reducible on 30 days' notice, and replaced the penalty with a true-up.

ops.newText: Customer's only purchase commitment is the amount stated in the applicable Order Form for the current twelve-month term, which Customer may reduce on thirty days' written notice. Any shortfall is settled by a true-up invoice for the unmet committed amount, and no penalty or take-or-pay charge applies. This Section does not limit Customer's termination rights.
ops.oldText: Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.

proposal.summary: Limit the commitment to 12 months, reducible on notice, with a true-up instead of take-or-pay.

quote: Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.
rationale: Section 2.1 is a multi-year take-or-pay with no reduction or termination right — expressly walk-away territory — and it contradicts Section 12.3's acknowledgement that no minimum-volume commitment has been made. Narrowed to the fallback: commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up instead of a penalty.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We accept only a narrow, mutual non-solicit: personnel actually involved in the Services, 12 months, with carve-outs for general advertising and unsolicited approaches, and no no-hire. The current 24-month all-employee no-hire also conflicts with Section 12.3.

ops.newText: During the term and for twelve months after the end of an individual's involvement in the Services, neither Party shall knowingly solicit for employment any of the other Party's personnel who were directly involved in providing or receiving the Services. This does not restrict general advertisements or other recruitment not targeted at those personnel, responses to them, unsolicited approaches by an individual, or the hiring of any person so identified.
ops.oldText: Customer shall not solicit, hire, or employ any Vendor employee during the term or for twenty-four months afterward, regardless of how the employee applies.

proposal.summary: Narrow the non-solicit to a mutual 12-month, involved-personnel restriction with carve-outs; delete the no-hire.

quote: Customer shall not solicit, hire, or employ any Vendor employee during the term or for twenty-four months afterward, regardless of how the employee applies.
rationale: This is a one-sided 24-month no-hire covering every Vendor employee with no general-advertising or unsolicited-approach carve-out — beyond the fallback and expressly a walk-away item — and inconsistent with Section 12.3. Narrowed to a mutual 12-month non-solicit of personnel directly involved in the Services with the standard carve-outs and no no-hire.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The agreement contains no exit obligations: Section 10.1 assumes a transition period that is never granted, and Section 16.5 points Customer Data to a Section 11 that does not exist. We have inserted our standard transition-assistance, data-return and deletion-certification paragraph (fallback: 90 days of assistance).

ops.text: Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement or an Order Form for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty days, return or export all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems, subject to routine backups and legal retention, and certify such deletion in writing.

proposal.summary: Insert transition assistance, data return within 30 days and certified deletion.

quote: On expiry or termination, Customer's right to access terminated subscription Services ends after any agreed transition period.
rationale: Section 10 deals only with access wind-down, Deliverable delivery and refunds; there is no transition-assistance obligation and no obligation to return or export Customer Data in a usable format (Section 16.5 defers Customer Data to a non-existent Section 11). For a hosted-services vendor this absence is a deviation, so we inserted the standard transition, data-return within 30 days and certified-deletion paragraph.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
